questions.title: Which drug is used as rescue therapy for sudden off-akinesia in Parkinson disease?
questions.question: A patient with advanced Parkinson disease develops a sudden, disabling "off" episode of akinesia despite regular oral levodopa. Which drug, given by subcutaneous injection, is used as rapid rescue therapy?

explanations.A: Correct. Apomorphine is a potent dopamine agonist given by subcutaneous injection; its rapid onset of action within minutes restores mobility during a sudden off-akinesia episode until the next dose of oral medication takes effect, making it the standard rescue therapy for this scenario. This rapid parenteral rescue role is a well-established exam point distinguishing apomorphine from the slower-onset oral antiparkinsonian agents used for maintenance therapy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Amantadine is an oral antiparkinsonian agent used for maintenance therapy or to reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesia, not as a rapid parenteral rescue drug for acute off-episodes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Benztropine is an oral anticholinergic used mainly for drug-induced extrapyramidal tremor, not for rescuing an off-akinesia episode.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Selegiline is an oral monoamine oxidase-B inhibitor used for maintenance therapy in early Parkinson disease, with a slow onset unsuitable for acute rescue.

questions.learning_objective: State that apomorphine is used as rescue therapy for sudden off-akinesia episodes in Parkinson disease.

questions.title: Buprenorphine acts at the mu-opioid receptor as which type of ligand?
questions.question: Buprenorphine is used both as an analgesic and in opioid substitution therapy. Which best describes its action at the mu-opioid receptor?

explanations.A: Correct. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor, meaning it only partially activates the receptor even at high doses, producing a ceiling effect on analgesia and respiratory depression and giving it a wider safety margin than full agonists. This partial-agonist ceiling effect is the pharmacological basis for buprenorphine's use in office-based opioid substitution therapy, where its safety margin in overdose is clinically valuable.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Morphine and methadone are full mu-agonists; buprenorphine's partial agonism, with its ceiling effect, is what distinguishes it from these drugs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Naloxone and naltrexone are competitive mu-receptor antagonists; buprenorphine still activates the receptor, distinguishing it from a pure antagonist.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An inverse agonist would reduce receptor activity below its baseline (constitutive) level; buprenorphine instead activates the receptor, just incompletely.

questions.learning_objective: State that buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, item 2 ("buprenorphine / Partial Mu Agonist"); identical fact also in CNS Assessment 1 Pharm item 1, held there as within-batch duplicate.

questions.title: Which characteristic adverse effect is associated with amantadine?
questions.question: A patient started on amantadine for Parkinson disease develops a mottled, lace-like reddish-blue skin discoloration of the legs. Which adverse effect is this?

explanations.A: Correct. Livedo reticularis, a mottled lace-like reddish-blue skin discoloration usually of the lower limbs, is a characteristic and distinctive adverse effect of amantadine, thought to relate to local catecholamine release affecting cutaneous vessels, and is generally reversible on stopping the drug. Recognising this drug-specific cutaneous sign helps distinguish amantadine from other antiparkinsonian agents whose adverse-effect profiles are otherwise quite different.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Orofacial dyskinesia is characteristic of tardive dyskinesia from chronic antipsychotic use, not amantadine.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Postural hypotension is more classically associated with levodopa or dopamine agonists, not the distinctive dermatological effect of amantadine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral neuropathy is not amantadine's characteristic adverse effect; its distinctive finding is the dermatological livedo reticularis.

questions.learning_objective: State that amantadine causes livedo reticularis as a characteristic adverse effect.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, item 3 ("amantadine / Livido reticularis")

questions.title: In which layer of the cerebellar cortex do mossy fibres synapse on granule cells?
questions.question: Mossy fibres are the major afferent input to the cerebellar cortex. In which of the cerebellar cortex's three layers do they synapse on granule cell dendrites?

explanations.A: Correct. Mossy fibres terminate in the innermost layer of the cerebellar cortex, the granular layer, where they synapse on the dendrites of granule cells to form characteristic glomeruli; they are not found in the molecular layer. This granular-layer synapse is the first stage of cerebellar cortical processing, upstream of the parallel-fibre input mossy fibres indirectly provide to Purkinje cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The molecular layer is where granule cell axons (as parallel fibres) synapse on Purkinje cell dendrites, along with climbing fibre synapses on Purkinje cells — mossy fibres themselves do not reach this layer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Purkinje cell layer is a single-cell-thick layer of Purkinje cell bodies between the molecular and granular layers; mossy fibres synapse on granule cells in the granular layer, not directly on Purkinje cell bodies.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cerebellar white matter lies deep to the three-layered cortex and contains axons, not the mossy fibre-granule cell synapse itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that mossy fibres synapse on granule cell dendrites in the granular layer of the cerebellar cortex.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, item 6 ("mossy fibers / Not found in the molecular layer of the the cerebellum cortex"); complementary to CNS Assessment 1 Histo item 2 ("Dentreties of granule cell Synapse with mossy fibers"), merged and held there.

questions.title: Which nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland?
questions.question: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the inferior salivatory nucleus synapse in the otic ganglion. Which nerve carries the resulting postganglionic fibres onward to the parotid gland?

explanations.A: Correct. The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, carries the postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion onward to the parotid gland, alongside its own sensory fibres. This two-step relay (preganglionic via the lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion, then postganglionic via the auriculotemporal nerve) is a classic head-and-neck anatomy exam sequence.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lesser petrosal nerve carries the preganglionic fibres to the otic ganglion, the step before, not the postganglionic fibres onward to the gland.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The chorda tympani carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular ganglion for the submandibular and sublingual glands, an entirely separate pathway from the parotid's.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The greater petrosal nerve carries preganglionic fibres to the pterygopalatine ganglion for the lacrimal gland, not the otic ganglion/parotid pathway.

questions.learning_objective: State that the auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland.

questions.title: Which fissure connects the infratemporal fossa to the pterygopalatine fossa?
questions.question: The maxillary artery and maxillary nerve branches pass from the infratemporal fossa into the pterygopalatine fossa through which fissure?

explanations.A: Correct. The pterygomaxillary fissure, between the posterior maxilla and the pterygoid process, is the opening through which the infratemporal fossa communicates with the pterygopalatine fossa, transmitting the terminal (third) part of the maxillary artery and maxillary nerve branches. This fissure's neurovascular contents make it a key landmark when tracing the maxillary artery and nerve from the infratemporal into the pterygopalatine fossa.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior orbital fissure connects the pterygopalatine fossa to the orbit, not the infratemporal fossa to the pterygopalatine fossa.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior orbital fissure connects the middle cranial fossa to the orbit, an entirely different communication.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no standard named "pterygoid fissure" serving this communication; the pterygomaxillary fissure is the correct named structure.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pterygomaxillary fissure connects the infratemporal fossa to the pterygopalatine fossa.

questions.title: Which is the only sensory branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve?
questions.question: The mandibular nerve's anterior division is mainly motor. Which nerve is the sole sensory exception, supplying the cheek?

explanations.A: Correct. The (long) buccal nerve is the only sensory branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve, supplying general sensation to the skin and mucosa of the cheek and the buccal gingiva of the lower molars. This exception to the anterior division's otherwise motor role is a frequently tested trigeminal nerve anatomy detail.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lingual nerve is a sensory branch of the posterior (mainly sensory) division of the mandibular nerve, not the anterior division.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The auriculotemporal nerve is also a branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve, not the anterior division.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior alveolar nerve is a branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve, carrying both sensory and motor (mylohyoid) fibres, not the anterior division.

questions.learning_objective: State that the buccal nerve is the only sensory branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve.

questions.title: Stimulation of the basal ganglia's indirect pathway has what effect on the subthalamic nucleus?
questions.question: Stimulation of the striatal neurons of the basal ganglia's indirect pathway has what net effect on the subthalamic nucleus?

explanations.A: Correct. Indirect-pathway striatal neurons inhibit the external globus pallidus (GPe), which normally tonically inhibits the subthalamic nucleus; inhibiting that inhibitory GPe drive disinhibits the subthalamic nucleus, increasing its activity. This disinhibition, in turn, increases excitatory drive from the subthalamic nucleus onto the internal globus pallidus, net-suppressing movement via the indirect pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The striatum does not project directly (via glutamate) to the subthalamic nucleus in the indirect pathway; its effect is indirect, via first inhibiting the GPe.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The subthalamic nucleus's activity does change — it increases, because the indirect pathway removes the GPe's inhibitory restraint on it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The striatum's GABAergic projection in this pathway targets the GPe, not the subthalamic nucleus directly, and the net effect on the subthalamic nucleus is disinhibition (increased, not decreased, activity).

questions.learning_objective: State that stimulation of the indirect pathway disinhibits the subthalamic nucleus.

questions.title: Above what approximate skin temperature do thermal nociceptors begin firing?
questions.question: Thermal (heat) nociceptor free nerve endings begin firing once skin temperature exceeds approximately which threshold?

explanations.A: Correct. Thermal nociceptors begin firing once skin temperature exceeds approximately 50 degC, the threshold marking the onset of a real risk of tissue damage, distinguishing them from ordinary non-painful warm thermoreceptors. This distinct, high threshold sets thermal nociceptors apart from the lower-threshold warm thermoreceptors that signal ordinary, non-painful temperature change.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 38 degC is within the normal, non-painful warm range signalled by warm thermoreceptors, well below the nociceptor threshold.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The warm (non-painful) thermoreceptor range extends up to around this level, but this is not the threshold at which pain-signalling thermal nociceptors themselves begin firing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 30 degC is within the normal ambient/skin temperature range, far below any nociceptive threshold.

questions.learning_objective: State that thermal nociceptors are stimulated by skin temperatures above about 50 degC.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, item 49 ("thermal nociceptors / stimulation to thermal noci receptors above 50"); identical fact also in CNS Assessment 1 Physio item 5, held there as within-batch duplicate.

questions.title: Which condition is a recognised cause of extracranial headache?
questions.question: Which of the following is classified as an extracranial (rather than intracranial) cause of headache?

explanations.A: Correct. Otitis media, inflammation of the middle ear, is a classic extracranial cause of headache: pain from the inflamed, pressurised middle ear is perceived as headache through the ear's sensory innervation, without any intracranial mechanism. Recognising extracranial causes such as this is important clinically, since they are treated by addressing the local structure rather than by intracranial headache management.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Meningeal irritation is an intracranial cause of headache, arising from pain-sensitive structures inside the skull, not an extracranial one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Decreased CSF pressure (as in a post-lumbar-puncture headache) is an intracranial cause of headache, related to traction on intracranial pain-sensitive structures, not an extracranial cause.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cerebral vasodilation (as in a migraine attack) is an intracranial vascular cause of headache, not an extracranial one.

questions.learning_objective: State that otitis media is a recognised cause of extracranial headache.
